extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy; scholars interested in Montesquieu and theories of law, religion, and public moeurs
extracted.subtask_description: Excerpts from Montesquieu's De l'Esprit des lois (with explanatory notes) describing political principles about how laws form manners, the proper relation of laws to religion, and the effects of legal penalties. Useful for studying normative rules about legislation, religious toleration, and civic character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Customs reflect political condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Les coutumes d'un peuple esclave sont une partie de sa servitude; celles d'un peuple libre sont une partie de sa liberté.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montesquieu treats customs (moeurs) as constitutive of a people's political state: customs of servitude reinforce servitude; customs of freedom reinforce liberty. This is presented as a general principle linking social practices to political condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws shape manners and character of a nation
rubrics_metrics.description: Comment les lois peuvent contribuer à former les moeurs, les manières et le caractère d'une nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter argues that laws do not merely follow customs but actively form them—affecting citizens' passions, habits, political behavior, commerce, military orientation, and cultural production. The text explains mechanisms (division of powers, public trust in legislature, incentives from executive control of offices) by which laws influence moeurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require mutual tolerance among religions when several are permitted
rubrics_metrics.description: Lorsque les lois d'un État ont cru devoir souffrir plusieurs religions, il faut qu'elles les obligent aussi à se tolérer entre elles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montesquieu asserts a civil-law requirement: permitting multiple religions must be accompanied by legal obligations of mutual toleration. A citizen must not only refrain from disturbing the state, but also must not disturb any other citizen. Rationale: religions repressed tend to become repressive when they gain power.

rubrics_metrics.name: If state accepts an established religion, do not allow establishment of another
rubrics_metrics.description: Comme il n'y a guère que les religions intolérantes qui aient un grand zèle pour s'établir ailleurs... ce sera une très bonne loi civile, lorsque l'État est satisfait de la religion déjà établie, de ne point souffrir l'établissement d'une autre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montesquieu recommends the civil-law rule that a state which is satisfied with its established religion should forbid the establishment of a different religion (he notes an exception in the chapter regarding Christianity in his argument). He grounds this in the observation that intolerant religions are most eager to spread by establishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sovereignly-initiated changes to a dominant religion
rubrics_metrics.description: Un prince qui entreprend dans son État de détruire ou de changer la religion dominante s'expose beaucoup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A ruler who tries to destroy or change the dominant religion risks revolution because religion is intertwined with the constitution and manners of the state; abrupt official changes produce distrust and bad citizens/faithful. Practical guidance: avoid top-down forcible religious reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid penal laws in matters of religion
rubrics_metrics.description: Il faut éviter les lois pénales en fait de religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penal laws inspire fear, but since religion already imposes its own sanctions, secular penalties interact with religious fears to 'make souls atrocious.' Montesquieu argues penal laws about religion have historically produced destruction rather than conversion or civic advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use invitations/incentives, not punishments, to change religion
rubrics_metrics.description: Règle générale: en fait de changement de religion, les invitations sont plus fortes que les peines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montesquieu counsels that to weaken or supplant a religion, the state should rely on favors, comforts, and the inducements of life and fortune rather than on threats and punishments; historical examples (e.g., persecutions in Japan) show cruelty provokes revolt, while long, moderate penalties tend to fatigue rather than convert.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repression begets reciprocal repression
rubrics_metrics.description: C'est un principe, que toute religion qui est réprimée devient elle-même réprimante; car sitôt que, par quelque hasard, elle peut sortir de l'oppression, elle attaque la religion qui l'a réprimée.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montesquieu offers a general causal rule: persecuting a religion tends to make it, when empowered, persecutory in turn. This is used to justify legal requirements of mutual toleration and to argue against coercive establishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clergy should rely on persuasion and moral example rather than force
rubrics_metrics.description: Ce clergé ne pouvant pas protéger la religion, ni être protégé par elle, sans force pour contraindre, chercherait à persuader: on verrait sortir de sa plume de très bons ouvrages, pour prouver la révélation et la providence du grand Être.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If civil power does not protect the clergy, the clergy's appropriate method is persuasion, cultivation of respect by moral conduct, learned writing, and example. Montesquieu predicts lower clerical credit but a higher emphasis on teaching and moral purity instead of coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative trust calms popular fears and corrects misinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Mais le corps législatif ayant la confiance du peuple, et étant plus éclairé que lui, il pourrait le faire revenir des mauvaises impressions qu'on lui aurait données et calmer ses mouvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montesquieu holds that a trusted, enlightened legislature can dissipate unjust fears stirred by opponents of the executive and thereby prevent destabilizing popular agitation. Practical implication: laws and institutional design should aim to build legislative trust to moderate factional alarmism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not violate fundamental laws; such violation provokes catastrophic revolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Mais, si elles naissaient à l'occasion du renversement des lois fondamentales, elles seraient sourdes, funestes, atroces, et produiraient des catastrophes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montesquieu warns that when public terrors or agitations arise from threats to fundamental laws, the resulting movements are deadly and destructive. Hence protecting fundamental constitutional laws is critical to avoid violent upheaval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of speech: citizens may say or write what laws do not expressly forbid
rubrics_metrics.description: pour jouir de la liberté, il faut que chacun puisse dire qu'il pense, et que, pour la conserver, il faut encore que chacun puisse dire ce qu'il pense... dirait et écrirait tout ce que les lois ne lui ont pas défendu expressément de dire ou d'écrire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montesquieu articulates a legal standard for liberty of expression: laws should permit citizens to speak and write freely except where something is expressly prohibited. The implication is a presumption in favor of free expression in a free polity.
